In the example below, we show how the metabolic rate of a typically-sized reptile varies as a function of its body temperature.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# Animal geometry (cm)
height <- 12 # height (cm)
width <- 8 # width (cm)
len <- 25 # length (cm)

# Create ectotherm parameter set
ecto_params <- micropoint::create_ectop(height,
                                        width,
                                        len,
                                        refl = 0.1, # body reflectance
                                        adir = 0, # orientation angle (degrees)
                                        position = "randomdir", # random orientation
                                        type = "reptile") # ectotherm type

# Assign variable body temperature
Tbody <- seq(-5, 60, length.out = 100) # body temperature (°C)

# Compute metabolic rate
met_rate <- with(ecto_params,
                 metabolic_rate(volume, # body volume (m^3)
                                rho, # body density (kg m^-3)
                                Q10, # temperature sensitivity coefficient
                                a0, # allometric intercept
                                b, # allometric exponent
                                Tref, # reference temperature (°C)
                                Tbody))

# ----------------------------- Plot results ------------------------------ #
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plot(met_rate ~ Tbody,
     type = "l",
     col = "red",
     lwd = 2,
     xlab = expression("Body temperature (" * degree * "C)"),
     ylab = expression("Metabolic rate (W)"))
```
![](images/img32.png)

### Ectotherms
The components described above are combined in the `Ectothermtemp` function, which solves for ectotherm body temperature at a single time step from animal traits, time and location, and a set of local microclimate variables. The required animal properties are supplied via the ecto_params object returned by create_ectop, while microcdata provides the near-body environmental conditions, including air and surface temperature, humidity, wind speed and direction, and the upward and downward shortwave and longwave fluxes.

The function first calculates solar position from time, latitude and longitude, and uses this together with body geometry and orientation to determine the fraction of direct solar radiation intercepted. Absorbed shortwave and longwave radiation are then calculated from the relevant flux components, accounting for surface reflectance and emissivity. The same body geometry is then used to compute the characteristic dimension relevant to convective heat exchange, by treating the wind as a horizontal beam and calculating projected area normal to the flow.

Body temperature is obtained iteratively because several terms depend on body temperature itself. At each iteration the function updates the boundary layer resistance to heat loss, metabolic heat production, radiative emission, sensible heat exchange, conductive exchange with the substrate, and latent heat exchange from exposed and contacting surfaces. These terms are then combined to give an updated estimate of body temperature, and iteration continues until the change between successive estimates falls below the specified tolerance.

This is a single-time-step calculation, so to predict body temperature through time it must be called repeatedly using time-varying microclimate inputs. In practice, this means first running the microclimate model to obtain the local conditions experienced by the animal, and then passing these to Ectothermtemp at each time step.

The example below illustrates this workflow for a small reptile on bare ground. We first subset the weather data to June, set the ground to bare and define the soil properties, and initialise the soil heat model. We then create the ectotherm parameter list, specifying body dimensions, reflectance and orientation assumptions. At each hourly time step the ground surface energy balance and the soil model are run to estimate the local microclimate, including near-surface air temperature and humidity, surface temperature, and the relevant radiative fluxes. These are assembled into a `microcdata` list and passed to `Ectothermtemp`, which returns body temperature for that hour.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# -------------------- Create June weather dataset ------------------------- #
# Reload the weather dataset: the name climdata is reused for model driving variables
climdata <- microclimlearn::climdata
weather <- climdata

# Select data for June
tme <- as.POSIXlt(weather$obs_time, tz = "UTC")
sel <- which(tme$mon + 1 == 6)
weather <- weather[sel,]
tme <- tme[sel]

# -------------------- Create vegetation parameter set -------------------- #
# Bare ground
vegp <- createplant_inputs("C3")
vegp$h <- 0     # vegetation height (m): zero for bare ground
vegp$pai <- 0   # plant area index: zero for bare ground

# -------------------- Create soil datasets and initialise models --------- #
groundp <- micropoint::groundparams

# Lower soil boundary temperature
boundaryT <- 11.36071

soilp <- createsoilplist(
  soiltype = "Clay loam",
  nlayers = 15,
  totalDepth = 2,
  slope = 0,
  aspect = 180,
  surface_organicmu = 1,
  FreeDrain = TRUE
)

# Number of soil layers
n <- length(soilp$b)

# Initial soil temperature profile
Te <- seq(weather$temp[1], boundaryT, length.out = n)

# Initial soil water content profile
theta <- seq(0.2, soilp$Smax[n], length.out = n)

# Initialise soil heat model
soilheat <- InitSoilheatmod(soilp, Te, theta)

# -------------------- Create ectotherm parameter set --------------------- #
ecto_params <- micropoint::create_ectop(
  height = 12,
  width = 8,
  len = 25,
  refl = 0.1,
  adir = 0,
  position = "randomdir",
  type = "reptile"
)

# -------------------- Run model in hourly timesteps ---------------------- #
Tbody <- G <- Tsurface <- 0

for (hr in 1:720) {

  # Initialise convergence criterion
  error <- 1e99
  itr <- 1

  # Iteratively solve canopy and soil energy balance
  while (error > 1e-2 && itr < 20) {

    # -------------------- Run microclimate model ------------------------ #

    # Estimate relative humidity at soil surface (percentage)
    soilrh <- soilrelhum(
      0.2,              # volumetric water content at the surface
      soilheat$Te[1],   # soil surface temperature (°C)
      soilp$psi_e[1],   # air-entry water potential (J/kg)
      soilp$b[1],       # Campbell shape parameter
      soilp$Smax[1]     # water content at saturation
    )

    # Solve the energy balance of the ground surface
    can <- solve_wholecanopy(
      weather,
      vegp,
      groundp,
      hr,
      49.96807,
      -5.215668,
      zref = 2,
      G,
      theta = 0.2,
      soilrh = soilrh
    )

    # -------------------- Solve soil heat transport --------------------- #

    soilheat <- SoilHeatModel(
      soilheat,
      soilp,
      Rabs = can$Rabs,               # radiation absorbed by the ground
      Tref = weather$temp[hr],
      relhum = weather$relhum[hr],
      atmPressure = weather$pres[hr],
      rHa = can$rHg                  # resistance from ground to zref
    )

    # Update convergence criterion
    error <- abs(G - soilheat$Gflux)
    G <- soilheat$Gflux
    itr <- itr + 1
  }

  # Move the soil model on to the next time step
  soilheat$oldTe <- soilheat$Te

  # --------- Calculate conditions 6 cm above the ground surface --------- #

  # Resistance to heat transfer between the ground surface and 6 cm
  r6 <- canopyresistance(0.06, can$uf, vegp$h, vegp$pai, can$LL)

  # Air temperature at 6 cm: the share of the temperature difference between
  # ground and reference height that lies above 6 cm
  Tz <- weather$temp[hr] +
    (can$tcanopy - weather$temp[hr]) *
    ((can$rHa - r6) / can$rHa)

  # Vapour pressures
  es <- satvap(can$tcanopy)
  ea <- satvap(weather$temp[hr]) *
    (weather$relhum[hr] / 100)

  # Vapour pressure at 6 cm, where vapour from the ground also meets the
  # resistance of the soil surface
  ez <- ea +
    (es - ea) *
    (can$rHa - r6) / (can$rHa + can$rS)

  # Relative humidity at 6 cm
  Rhz <- pmin((ez / satvap(Tz)) * 100, 100)

  # Wind speed at 6 cm
  uz <- windprofile_above(0.06, can$uf, vegp$h, vegp$pai, can$LL)

  # --------- Calculate upward and downward radiation fluxes ------------ #

  # Solar geometry
  solp <- sunposition(
    tme[hr],
    lat = 49.96807,
    long = -5.215668
  )

  # Surface albedo
  albs <- albedo(
    vegp$pai,
    vegp$lref,
    vegp$ltra,
    vegp$x,
    groundp$gref,
    groundp$slope,
    groundp$aspect,
    solp
  )

  # Compute direct and reflected shortwave radiation
  if (weather$swdown[hr] > 0) {

    Rdirdown <- (weather$swdown[hr] -
      weather$difrad[hr]) /
      cos(solp$zen * pi / 180)

    Rswup <- albs$albd * weather$difrad[hr] +
      Rdirdown * cos(solp$zen * pi / 180) *
      albs$albb

  } else {

    Rdirdown <- Rswup <- 0
  }

  # ---------------- Calculate ectotherm body temperature --------------- #

  microcdata <- list(
    Tair = Tz,
    Tsurf = can$tcanopy,
    relhum = Rhz,
    surfrelhum = soilrh,
    pk = weather$pres[hr],
    windspeed = uz,
    winddir = weather$winddir[hr],
    Rdirdown = Rdirdown,
    Rdifdown = weather$difrad[hr],
    Rswup = Rswup,
    Rlwdown = weather$lwdown[hr],
    # longwave emitted by the ground and sky longwave it reflects
    Rlwup = groundp$em * 5.67e-8 * (can$tcanopy + 273.15)^4 +
      (1 - groundp$em) * weather$lwdown[hr]
  )

  # Solve ectotherm heat balance
  Tbody[hr] <- Ectothermtemp(
    ecto_params,
    tme[hr],
    microcdata,
    lat = 49.96807,
    long = -5.215668
  )
}

# ------------------------- Plot temperatures ----------------------------- #
tmec <- as.POSIXct(tme)

# Air temperature
plot(
  weather$temp ~ tmec,
  type = "l",
  xlab = "Date",
  ylab = "Temperature (°C)",
  ylim = c(0, 50),
  col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.5),
  lwd = 2
)

# Ectotherm body temperature
par(new = TRUE)

plot(
  Tbody ~ tmec,
  type = "l",
  xlab = "",
  ylab = "",
  ylim = c(0, 50),
  col = "red"
)

# Add legend
legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c("Air temperature", "Body temperature"),
  col = c(rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.5), "red"),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n"
)
```
![](images/img33.png)

Body temperature is predicted from the local conditions experienced by the animal near the ground, not directly from standard weather data. The microclimate model is therefore used first to translate reference-height meteorological observations into temperature, humidity and radiative conditions at the animal’s height, and these are then passed to Ectothermtemp.

In the final plot, the red line shows predicted body temperature and the grey line the air temperature at 2 m from the weather data. Differences between the two arise because the animal exchanges heat not only with the air, but also by radiation and by conduction with the ground it rests on.

The microcdata object contains the quantities needed for this calculation: air temperature and humidity at the animal’s height (Tair, relhum), surface temperature, the humidity of the ground surface and upward longwave flux from below (Tsurf, surfrelhum, Rlwup), and the direct, diffuse and reflected shortwave components (Rdirdown, Rdifdown, Rswup).

### Endotherms
Birds and mammals maintain a relatively stable core temperature by regulating heat production and loss. Their thermal balance differs from that of an ectotherm because the temperature of the body surface can be very different from that of the core. Heat moves between the core and the environment through body tissues and the coat of fur or feathers, before being exchanged with the surroundings by convection and radiation. Each stage offers resistance to heat flow. In steady state, heat flow through these successive resistances is analogous to current through electrical resistors in series: the greater the resistance, the larger the temperature difference needed to carry a given heat flux. Thus, the surface of a well-insulated coat can be much cooler than the animal's core, and it is this outer surface that exchanges sensible and radiative heat with the surroundings.

The coat resistance, calculated by `coatresistance`, is its depth divided by its effective thermal conductivity. The latter includes heat conducted through the air and hairs or feathers, as well as radiative transfer within the coat. `tissueresistance` represents the resistance between core and skin, taking account of heat produced within the body. Its value depends on body size and tissue conductivity, which can vary as blood vessels near the skin constrict or dilate. Beyond the coat, convection and radiation act in parallel. `operativetemp` combines these exchanges using the convective boundary-layer resistance calculated by `animalrHa` and an equivalent radiative resistance. It returns both an external resistance and the operative temperature: the temperature of a uniform environment that would produce the same combined convective and radiative heat exchange with the coat surface. When the radiative surroundings are at air temperature and there is no absorbed shortwave radiation, operative temperature equals air temperature. In sunshine, it can be substantially higher.

`Endotherm` combines these resistances to calculate the heat that must be produced or dissipated to maintain core temperature. Heat transfer between the core and the surroundings depends on the difference between core and operative temperature and the sum of the resistances; breathing also removes heat and water vapour. Three broad responses are possible. Below the thermoneutral zone, even maximum tissue insulation is insufficient to retain the heat generated by basal metabolism, so metabolic heat production must increase. Within the thermoneutral zone, basal metabolism is sufficient and heat loss can be regulated by changing blood flow to the skin. Above it, sensible and radiative exchange cannot dispose of basal heat production even at minimum tissue resistance, so additional evaporative cooling is required, through panting or sweating where available. `Endotherm` returns the required metabolic rate, the evaporative loss needed to maintain core temperature, the maximum evaporative capacity, and the temperatures of the skin and coat surface. Evaporation can be expressed as heat loss (W), water loss (litres per day), or a percentage of body mass per day.

The function also returns physiologically equivalent temperature (`PET`). Originally developed as a human thermal index (Höppe 1999), PET expresses the combined effects of temperature, radiation and wind as the air temperature of a standard reference environment that would produce an equivalent physiological thermal state. Unlike air temperature, PET therefore depends on the properties of the animal as well as its surroundings.

Animal parameters are assembled by `create_endop`. The user supplies body dimensions, coat depth, animal type (bird or mammal), and relevant attributes such as reflectance and sweating ability. Default physiological parameters come from published relationships: basal metabolic rate is estimated from mass using Kleiber's (1947) relation, while core temperature, allowable tissue conductivity, skin wetness and panting capacity draw on the `NicheMapR` endotherm model (Kearney et al. 2021). The default coat conductivity is based on measurements of cattle hair (Maia et al. 2009). This is a simplification: coat structure and insulation vary between species, although the broadly proportional relationship between coat depth and insulation reported by Scholander et al. (1950) provides some justification. Defaults can be changed in the returned parameter list.

We illustrate the model with two contrasting mammals: a roughly 200 kg lion with a short coat and a roughly 40 g rodent. First, we calculate the lion's skin and coat-surface temperatures at an air temperature of 20 °C, in shade and in full sun.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# ----------------------- Create endotherm parameters ----------------------- #
lion <- create_endop(height = 55,    # body height (cm)
                     width = 40,     # body width (cm)
                     len = 170,      # body length (cm)
                     coat = 0.5,     # coat depth (cm)
                     type = "mammal",
                     refl = 0.3,     # reflectance of the coat
                     adir = 90,      # facing east
                     position = "fixed")
lion$Tb <- 38.5 # core temperature of a lion (°C)

rodent <- create_endop(height = 3, width = 3, len = 8, coat = 0.5,
                       type = "mammal", adir = 90, position = "fixed")

# ------------------ Function to set up simple conditions ------------------- #
# Air temperature tair, direct radiation Rdir (W m^-2), wind speed u (m s^-1),
# with longwave radiation from the sky and ground that of surroundings at air
# temperature
conditions <- function(tair, Rdir, u) {
  sb <- 5.67e-8 # Stefan-Boltzmann constant
  list(Tair = tair,
       relhum = 50,
       pk = 101.3,
       windspeed = u,
       winddir = 0, # wind from the north, side-on to the animal
       Rdirdown = Rdir,
       Rdifdown = 0.2 * Rdir,
       Rswup = 0.2 * Rdir,
       Rlwdown = sb * (tair + 273.15)^4,
       Rlwup = sb * (tair + 273.15)^4)
}

# Midday on 21 June, latitude 50 °N
tme <- as.POSIXlt("2025-06-21 12:00", tz = "UTC")

# -------------- Lion at 20 °C, wind 1 m/s, in shade and in sun ------------- #
shade <- Endotherm(lion, tme, conditions(20, 0, 1), lat = 50, long = 0)
sun <- Endotherm(lion, tme, conditions(20, 800, 1), lat = 50, long = 0)
round(c(Tskin = shade$Tskin, Tsurf = shade$Tsurf), 1)
round(c(Tskin = sun$Tskin, Tsurf = sun$Tsurf), 1)
```

In shade, the lion's skin is predicted to be about 34 °C, while the outer coat is about 26 °C, much closer to air temperature. In full sun, the coat surface reaches about 40 °C, exceeding core temperature. The direction of heat flow through the coat can then reverse: rather than limiting heat loss from the body, the coat limits heat gain from its sun-warmed surface.

We next compare the effects of wind and solar radiation on PET for the lion and rodent.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# -------------------- Equivalent temperature against wind ------------------ #
u <- seq(0.1, 5, length.out = 50) # wind speed (m s^-1)
PET_lion <- PET_rodent <- numeric(length(u))
for (i in seq_along(u)) {
  PET_lion[i] <- Endotherm(lion, tme, conditions(10, 0, u[i]), 50, 0)$PET
  PET_rodent[i] <- Endotherm(rodent, tme, conditions(10, 0, u[i]), 50, 0)$PET
}

# ------------------ Equivalent temperature against radiation --------------- #
Rad <- seq(0, 800, 50) # direct radiation (W m^-2), shade to full sun
PETr_lion <- PETr_rodent <- numeric(length(Rad))
for (i in seq_along(Rad)) {
  PETr_lion[i] <- Endotherm(lion, tme, conditions(20, Rad[i], 1), 50, 0)$PET
  PETr_rodent[i] <- Endotherm(rodent, tme, conditions(20, Rad[i], 1), 50, 0)$PET
}

# ----------------------------- Plot results ------------------------------ #
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(PET_lion ~ u, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(-15, 15),
     xlab = expression("Wind speed (m s"^-1 * ")"),
     ylab = expression("Equivalent temperature (" * degree * "C)"))
lines(PET_rodent ~ u, lwd = 2, col = "red")
abline(h = 10, lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Lion", "Rodent", "Air temperature"),
       col = c("black", "red", "black"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
plot(PETr_lion ~ Rad, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(10, 50),
     xlab = expression("Direct radiation (W m"^-2 * ")"),
     ylab = expression("Equivalent temperature (" * degree * "C)"))
lines(PETr_rodent ~ Rad, lwd = 2, col = "red")
abline(h = 20, lty = 2)
```
![](images/img33a.png)

Without solar radiation and as wind approaches zero, PET approaches air temperature for both animals. Increasing wind lowers PET, particularly for the rodent: at 5 m s^-1^, PET is about 12 °C below air temperature for the rodent, compared with about 7 °C for the lion. Wind reduces the insulating effect of the boundary layer around the animal. This external resistance makes a larger contribution to the rodent's total thermal resistance, whereas the lion is less sensitive to the same change in wind speed. Increasing radiation has the opposite effect. Under the conditions simulated, PET rises by about 23 °C for the lion and 14 °C for the rodent. Note that our simple `conditions` function increases diffuse and reflected shortwave radiation along with the direct beam, so the second panel represents increasing overall solar exposure rather than a change in direct radiation alone.

We can also use `Endotherm` to identify the thermoneutral zone, within which basal heat production is sufficient to maintain core temperature without additional evaporative cooling. The next example calculates metabolic heat production and evaporative water loss across a range of shaded air temperatures. Expressing these as a multiple of basal metabolic rate and as a percentage of body mass per day makes the two animals easier to compare.

```{r eval=FALSE}
tair <- seq(-10, 40, 1) # air temperature (°C)
M_lion <- M_rodent <- E_lion <- E_rodent <- numeric(length(tair))
for (i in seq_along(tair)) {
  out_lion <- Endotherm(lion, tme, conditions(tair[i], 0, 1), 50, 0, evapunits = "percent")
  out_rodent <- Endotherm(rodent, tme, conditions(tair[i], 0, 1), 50, 0, evapunits = "percent")
  M_lion[i] <- out_lion$Mreq / out_lion$Mbasal
  M_rodent[i] <- out_rodent$Mreq / out_rodent$Mbasal
  E_lion[i] <- out_lion$Ereq
  E_rodent[i] <- out_rodent$Ereq
}

# ----------------------------- Plot results ------------------------------ #
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(M_lion ~ tair, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 8),
     xlab = expression("Air temperature (" * degree * "C)"),
     ylab = "Metabolic rate (multiple of basal)")
lines(M_rodent ~ tair, lwd = 2, col = "red")
legend("topright", legend = c("Lion", "Rodent"), col = c("black", "red"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
plot(E_lion ~ tair, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 40),
     xlab = expression("Air temperature (" * degree * "C)"),
     ylab = "Evaporation (% of body mass per day)")
lines(E_rodent ~ tair, lwd = 2, col = "red")
```
![](images/img33b.png)

The lion's predicted thermoneutral zone extends from roughly 13 to 22 °C. Below this range, its metabolic rate increases relatively slowly, remaining below twice basal even at −10 °C. The rodent has a much narrower thermoneutral range, centred near 31 °C. Below this, it must increase metabolic heat production sharply, reaching nearly eight times basal at −10 °C. Such high expenditure would be difficult to sustain, which helps explain the importance of behavioural thermoregulation in small mammals, including huddling, curling up and using burrows. At high temperatures, both animals require evaporative cooling. Relative to body mass, the rodent's requirement rises much more rapidly, approaching 40% of its mass per day at 40 °C. This reflects its high surface-area-to-volume ratio and the scale of evaporative loss relative to its small water reserve. Evaporation also occurs in the cold through respiration, particularly when metabolic demand, and hence breathing, is high.

Finally, we examine how the lion's heat load varies over a month, comparing full sun with shade. The supplied weather dataset comes from southwest England, so we modify June conditions to create an illustrative, warmer and sunnier environment. These are synthetic weather conditions, not observations from an African site. The example also introduces `clearskyrad`, which estimates incoming shortwave radiation under clear skies, and `difprop`, which estimates the diffuse fraction of incoming shortwave radiation.

We add 12 °C to air temperature and recalculate relative humidity while keeping actual vapour pressure constant. We then slightly reduce effective sky emissivity to represent clearer conditions, recalculate downward longwave radiation, and halve wind speed. To adjust sunshine, we express the observed shortwave flux as a proportion of the clear-sky estimate from `clearskyrad`, increase that proportion using a logit transformation, and apply it to a new clear-sky estimate for the altered conditions and location. Finally, `difprop` partitions the resulting incoming shortwave radiation into diffuse and direct components.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# -------------------------- Select June weather ---------------------------- #
# Reload the weather dataset: the name climdata is reused for model driving variables
climdata <- microclimlearn::climdata
weather <- climdata
# Extract time and subset to June
tme <- as.POSIXlt(weather$obs_time, tz = "UTC")
sel <- which(tme$mon + 1 == 6)
weather <- weather[sel, ]
tme <- tme[sel]

# -------------------------- Helper functions ------------------------------- #
# Logit transforms used to adjust bounded variables (0–1)
logit <- function(x) log(x / (1 - x))
inv_logit <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))

# -------------------------- Adjust temperature & humidity ------------------ #
# Increase temperature to represent warmer (e.g. tropical) conditions
temp_new <- weather$temp + 12
# Recalculate relative humidity assuming constant vapour pressure
ea <- satvap(weather$temp) * (weather$relhum / 100)
relhum_new <- (ea / satvap(temp_new)) * 100

# -------------------------- Adjust longwave radiation ---------------------- #
# Derive sky emissivity from observed longwave radiation
skyem <- weather$lwdown / (5.67e-8 * (weather$temp + 273.15)^4)
# Reduce emissivity slightly (clearer skies → lower emissivity)
skyem_new <- inv_logit(logit(skyem) - 0.3)

# Recalculate downward longwave radiation using updated emissivity and temperature
lwdown_new <- skyem_new * 5.67e-8 * (temp_new + 273.15)^4

# Assemble updated weather object
weather_new <- weather
weather_new$temp <- temp_new
weather_new$relhum <- relhum_new
weather_new$lwdown <- lwdown_new
weather_new$windspeed <- 0.5 * weather$windspeed

# -------------------------- Adjust shortwave radiation --------------------- #
# Compute clear-sky radiation for original conditions
csr <- clearskyrad(weather, 49.96807, -5.215668)

# Calculate clear-sky fraction
csf <- weather$swdown / csr

# Increase clearness (make conditions sunnier) using logit transform
csf_new <- inv_logit(logit(csf) + 0.3)

# Recompute clear-sky radiation for new (warmer) conditions and location
csr_new <- clearskyrad(weather_new, -1.21867, -5.215668)

# Apply adjusted clear-sky fraction
weather_new$swdown <- csf_new * csr_new

# Ensure nighttime and invalid values are handled
weather_new$swdown[weather$swdown == 0] <- 0
weather_new$swdown[is.na(weather_new$swdown)] <- 0

# -------------------------- Partition into diffuse radiation --------------- #
# Compute diffuse fraction based on solar geometry and atmospheric conditions
diffrac <- difprop(weather_new, -1.21867, -5.215668)

# Calculate diffuse shortwave radiation
weather_new$difrad <- diffrac * weather_new$swdown
```

As in the ectotherm example, we first calculate the ground energy balance and near-surface microclimate, here for bare ground and at 30 cm above the surface, approximately the height of the lion's body centre. We estimate air temperature and wind at that height, and vapour pressure there from the small amount of water evaporating from the dry soil surface. For each hour, `Endotherm` is run in full sun and again with the direct beam removed to represent shade. Diffuse skylight, reflected shortwave radiation and longwave exchange are left unchanged; this isolates the effect of blocking direct sunlight rather than simulating the full microclimate beneath a tree.

```{r eval=FALSE}
# -------------------- Ground and soil ---------------------------------------- #
vegp <- createplant_inputs("C3")
vegp$h <- 0     # bare ground
vegp$pai <- 0
groundp <- micropoint::groundparams
lat <- -1.21867
long <- -5.215668
soilp <- createsoilplist(soiltype = "Clay loam", nlayers = 15, totalDepth = 2,
                         slope = 0, aspect = 180, surface_organicmu = 1,
                         FreeDrain = TRUE)
n <- length(soilp$b)
Te <- seq(weather_new$temp[1], 23.3, length.out = n) # 23.3 °C at the lower boundary
# Dry savanna soil: air-dry at the surface, moister at depth
theta <- seq(0.05, soilp$Smax[n], length.out = n)
soilheat <- InitSoilheatmod(soilp, Te, theta)

# ----------------------- Run model in hourly timesteps ---------------------- #
PET_sun <- PET_shade <- E_sun <- E_shade <- Emax <- Tz_all <- G <- 0
for (hr in 1:720) {
  error <- 1e99
  itr <- 1
  while (error > 1e-2 && itr < 20) {
    soilrh <- soilrelhum(0.05, soilheat$Te[1], soilp$psi_e[1], soilp$b[1], soilp$Smax[1])
    can <- solve_wholecanopy(weather_new, vegp, groundp, hr, lat, long, zref = 2,
                             G, theta = 0.05, soilrh = soilrh)
    soilheat <- SoilHeatModel(soilheat, soilp, Rabs = can$Rabs,
                              Tref = weather_new$temp[hr],
                              relhum = weather_new$relhum[hr],
                              atmPressure = weather_new$pres[hr], rHa = can$rHg)
    error <- abs(G - soilheat$Gflux)
    G <- soilheat$Gflux
    itr <- itr + 1
  }
  soilheat$oldTe <- soilheat$Te

  # ------------- Air temperature, humidity and wind at 30 cm --------------- #
  r30 <- canopyresistance(0.3, can$uf, vegp$h, vegp$pai, can$LL)
  Tz <- weather_new$temp[hr] +
    (can$tcanopy - weather_new$temp[hr]) * (can$rHa - r30) / can$rHa
  # Vapour evaporating from the ground raises the vapour pressure near the
  # surface, and its excess over that at 2 m falls off with height as heat does
  ea <- satvap(weather_new$temp[hr]) * (weather_new$relhum[hr] / 100)
  ez <- ea + (satvap(can$tcanopy) - ea) * (can$rHa - r30) / (can$rS + can$rHa)
  uz <- windprofile_above(0.3, can$uf, vegp$h, vegp$pai, can$LL)

  # ------------------- Direct and reflected shortwave ---------------------- #
  solp <- sunposition(tme[hr], lat, long)
  albs <- albedo(vegp$pai, vegp$lref, vegp$ltra, vegp$x, groundp$gref,
                 groundp$slope, groundp$aspect, solp)
  if (weather_new$swdown[hr] > 0) {
    Rdirdown <- (weather_new$swdown[hr] - weather_new$difrad[hr]) /
      cos(solp$zen * pi / 180)
    Rswup <- albs$albd * weather_new$difrad[hr] +
      Rdirdown * cos(solp$zen * pi / 180) * albs$albb
  } else {
    Rdirdown <- Rswup <- 0
  }

  # ------------------------- Lion in sun and in shade ----------------------- #
  microcdata <- list(Tair = Tz,
                     relhum = pmin(100 * ez / satvap(Tz), 100),
                     pk = weather_new$pres[hr],
                     windspeed = uz,
                     winddir = weather_new$winddir[hr],
                     Rdirdown = Rdirdown,
                     Rdifdown = weather_new$difrad[hr],
                     Rswup = Rswup,
                     Rlwdown = weather_new$lwdown[hr],
                     Rlwup = groundp$em * 5.67e-8 * (can$tcanopy + 273.15)^4 +
                       (1 - groundp$em) * weather_new$lwdown[hr])
  sun <- Endotherm(lion, tme[hr], microcdata, lat, long, evapunits = "L/day")
  microcdata$Rdirdown <- 0 # shade: direct beam blocked
  shade <- Endotherm(lion, tme[hr], microcdata, lat, long, evapunits = "L/day")
  PET_sun[hr] <- sun$PET
  PET_shade[hr] <- shade$PET
  E_sun[hr] <- sun$Ereq
  E_shade[hr] <- shade$Ereq
  Emax[hr] <- shade$Emax
  Tz_all[hr] <- Tz
}

# ----------------------------- Plot results ------------------------------ #
tmec <- as.POSIXct(tme)
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(PET_sun ~ tmec, type = "l", col = "red", ylim = c(10, 80),
     xlab = "Date", ylab = expression("Temperature (" * degree * "C)"))
lines(PET_shade ~ tmec, col = "blue")
lines(Tz_all ~ tmec, col = "darkgrey")
legend("topleft", legend = c("Equivalent temperature, sun",
                              "Equivalent temperature, shade", "Air temperature"),
       col = c("red", "blue", "darkgrey"), lwd = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
plot(E_sun ~ tmec, type = "l", col = "red", ylim = c(0, 20),
     xlab = "Date", ylab = expression("Evaporation (L day"^-1 * ")"))
lines(E_shade ~ tmec, col = "blue")
lines(Emax ~ tmec, lty = 2)
```
![](images/img34.png)

In full sun, the lion's predicted PET at midday rises as much as 25 °C above air temperature at 30 cm. Shade reduces this difference, but PET can still exceed air temperature by up to 16 °C. Blocking the direct beam does not remove radiation emitted or reflected by the hot ground. At night, PET drops a few degrees below air temperature as the animal loses radiant heat to the cooler sky.

The lower panel compares the evaporative water loss *required* to maintain the assumed fixed core temperature with the maximum rate available through the modelled cooling mechanisms (dashed line). For much of the middle of the day, the requirement exceeds that capacity in both sun and shade. At midday in sun, for example, the model predicts a requirement of roughly 9 litres per day against a capacity of about 3.2 litres per day. These are equivalent instantaneous rates, not the amount lost over an entire day. Where required evaporation exceeds capacity, the assumed steady core temperature cannot be maintained under these conditions. The animal would need to reduce heat gain, for example by resting on cooler ground in deeper shade, or allow core temperature to rise.

This is intentionally a simplified endotherm model. It holds core temperature fixed and uses a single body geometry and coat representation. A more detailed treatment could allow for changing posture, regional variation in the coat and transient body heat storage, as in the endotherm model implemented in `NicheMapR` (Kearney et al. 2021). For humans, related approaches underpin indices including PET, the Universal Thermal Climate Index and Wet Bulb Globe Temperature; simpler temperature–humidity indices are also widely used for livestock.

## Microclimate models

### micropoint
The `micropoint` package most closely replicates the modelling approaches outlined in this vignette. It is designed to derive microclimatic conditions or ectotherm body temperatures at single point locations and the majority of the functions are R wrappers for C++ code that replicates the R functions detailed in this vignette. It can thus be thought of as a fast version of the `microlearn` package designed for practical use. It supersedes the `microclimc` package (Maclean & Klinges 2021), updating the treatment of below-canopy microclimate processes and improving computational efficiency through the use of underlying C++ implementations.

The package is still in development, but is available for use with the disclaimer that, as the codebase is still evolving, stability and backward compatibility cannot yet be fully guaranteed.Currently two parallel versions of the package exist:

(1) a new version that uses the full multi-layer soil heat and water models described in this vignette. A tutorial for this version of the package is available from [here](https://rpubs.com/ilyamaclean/micropointnew).

(2) an older version of the package that implements the simpler approach to deriving ground heat flux described above, in which ground heat flux is assumed to follow a sinusoidal cycle that scales with the amplitude of the diurnal cycle in soil surface temperature. This version of the package also uses a simpler method for estimating stomatal conductance, relying on fewer vegetation parameters and assuming limitation primarily by photosynthetically active radiation rather than soil moisture. A tutorial for this version of the package is available form [here](https://rpubs.com/ilyamaclean/1262923)

Both versions of the package are bundled together and installed as detailed below. They simply use different functions to evoke the different versions

```{r eval=FALSE}
require(devtools) # Install from CRAN if not already installed
devtools::install_github("ilyamaclean/micropoint")
library(micropoint)
```

An example output generated by the new version of the package is shown below. Here microclimatic temperatures conditions are derived 5 cm above ground for a 10 cm grassland using the `micropoint::RunMicro` function over the course of a year (red) using the inbuilt climate dataset. Macroclimatic temperatures 2m above ground are shown in grey.

![](images/img35.png)

### microclimf
The `microclimf` package (Maclean 2026) extends `micropoint` to gridded applications and supersedes the microclimate components of the older package `microclima` (Maclean *et al* 2019) by modelling microclimate entirely form first principles. It allows microclimate models to be run efficiently across landscapes. A key challenge is that conventional microclimate models require iterative solutions at each location, which becomes computationally expensive when applied to many grid cells. The `microclimf` model addresses this by exploiting a near-linear relationship between errors in non-iterative surface temperature estimates and the corresponding air–surface temperature difference. In practice, the model is run iteratively at a single reference location, and the resulting relationships are then used to estimate temperatures across the rest of the grid without iteration. Additional efficiencies are achieved in the treatment of vegetation. Rather than resolving detailed vertical canopy structure, microclimf assumes that total sensible and latent heat fluxes can be represented at the canopy scale, and that vertical transfer profiles follow a generalised analytical form. This avoids the need for explicit multilayer canopy representation while retaining the key effects of vegetation on below-canopy microclimate.

Detailed instructions for using the package are provided [here](https://rpubs.com/ilyamaclean/runningmicroclimf). It is installed as follows:

```{r eval=FALSE}
require(devtools) # Install from CRAN if not already installed
devtools::install_github("ilyamaclean/microclimf")
library(microclimf)
```

An example output generated using `microclimf::runmicro_big` function the is shown below. Heretemperatures 5 cm above ground at 2 pm on 1 June 2017, modelled at 1m resolution for a 1×1km area around Caerthillian Cove, Cornwall, UK (49.968°N, 5.215°W). 

![](images/img36.png)

### mesoclim
So far, we have focused on the principles of microclimate modelling, deliberately excluding the downscaling of macroclimate data to finer spatial resolution. In other words, the emphasis has been on energy balance processes rather than adiabatic drivers of meso-scale climate variation, such as those associated with elevation or proximity to the coast. 

The `mesoclim` package is designed for climate downscaling. It provides functions to account for processes such as cold-air drainage, as well as elevation and water-body effects on climatic conditions measured at weather stations. It also includes tools for temporal downscaling of climate datasets and for bias correction of future climate projections. It also contains a range of functions for basic processing of climate datasets such as infilling of coastal grid cells. In effect, it provides the necessary climate forcing data required to run microclimate models. 

Detailed instructions for using the package are provided [here](to be added). It is installed as follows:

```{r eval=FALSE}
require(devtools) # Install from CRAN if not already installed
devtools::install_github("ilyamaclean/mesoclim")
library(mesoclim)
```

Below is an example figure generated with the aid of the the `mesoclim` package. It shows side-by-side comparisons of mesoclim output downscaled to 100 m resolution and the original 1 km HadCRU data from the UK Met Office. The maps depict the fraction of years in which the Isles of Scilly (a small island archipelago off southwest UK; 49.9°N, 6.3°W) experience a subtropical climate (defined as at least eight months with a mean temperature of 10^\circ C or above). In addition to resolving fine-scale spatial structure, the mesoclim output fills gaps where coarse-resolution data are absent, particularly around coastlines and small islands, producing spatially continuous and more realistic climatic surfaces.

![](images/img37.png)

### microclimdata and mcera5
One of the main practical challenges in microclimate modelling is obtaining and preparing the required climate forcing, as well as vegetation and terrain predictor variables. The `mcera5` package (Klinges et al. 2022) provides convenient access to, and processing of, ERA5 climate data (from the ECMWF Copernicus Climate Data Store) for use in microclimate models. It can be installed as follows, and the package includes its own vignette explaining how to download and prepare the data.

```{r eval=FALSE}
remotes::install_github(“dklinges9/mcera5”
library(mcera5)
```

The `microclimdata` package extends the capabilities of `mcera5`, enabling the download and processing of a wider range of climate datasets. It also provides tools for obtaining, processing, and generating the vegetation and soil data required for microclimate modelling, and for deriving the necessary model parameters. Together, these allow microclimate models to be run globally at spatial resolutions down to ~10 m.

Detailed instructions for using the package are provided [here](https://rpubs.com/ilyamaclean/microclimdataguide). It is installed as follows:

```{r eval=FALSE}
require(devtools) # Install from CRAN if not already installed
devtools::install_github("ilyamaclean/microclimdata")
library(microclimdata)
```

Below is an example illustrating the capabilities of `microclimdata`. The left panel shows a 10 m resolution mosaic of Leaf Area Index (LAI) over a 1 km² area in Cornwall, UK (50.1°N, 5.3°W), generated using the `lai_download` and `lai_mosaic` functions, prior to cloud filling. The right panel shows the same dataset after applying `lai_fill` to infill areas obscured by cloud.

![](images/img38.png)

### NicheMapR
The NicheMapR package (Kearney & Porter 2017) is a comprehensive biophysical modelling framework that links microclimate conditions to organismal heat, water and energy balance. It is built around a set of well-established Fortran models, wrapped in R, and is widely used for mechanistic niche modelling—that is, predicting where species can persist based on first-principles representations of how environmental conditions interact with organism physiology, rather than relying on statistical correlations with observed distributions.

The package comprises three main components. The microclimate model (Kearney & Porter 2017) predicts hourly above- and below-ground environmental conditions from meteorological, terrain and soil inputs, including soil temperature and moisture profiles. It also includes an explicit treatment of snow, allowing simulation of snow accumulation and melt and their effects on ground temperatures and thermal buffering during winter. The underlying processes and formulations are very similar to those described in this vignette—particularly for soil heat and water dynamics. The main difference is that below-canopy microclimate is not resolved explicitly; instead, canopy effects are represented more simply through a shading factor that modifies the amount of radiation reaching the ground. These outputs form the environmental inputs for the organism models.


The ectotherm model uses these microclimate predictions to solve the heat and water balance of ectothermic organisms, estimating body temperature, activity, water loss and behavioural responses based on specified morphological and physiological traits (Kearney & Porter 2019). The underlying heat balance is formulated in a very similar way to that described in this vignette. The model can also represent transient heat exchange, including single- and two-compartment (“lumped”) formulations that allow internal temperature gradients to be represented, which is important for larger organisms. It can be coupled to Dynamic Energy Budget (DEB) theory to simulate growth, development and reproduction through time. In simple terms, DEB models describe how organisms acquire energy from food and then use it—first to meet basic maintenance costs, and then, if sufficient energy remains, to support growth and reproduction—allowing physiological performance to be linked directly to environmental conditions.

The endotherm model extends this approach to homeothermic organisms, solving for the metabolic rate and water loss required to maintain a stable core body temperature under given environmental conditions (Kearney & Porter 2021). As in this vignette, it represents heat exchange between the organism and its environment, but goes further in its treatment of endotherm-specific physiology, explicitly accounting for traits such as fur or feather insulation and the temperatures of the body surface and insulating layer. Rather than providing a simple index of thermal stress, it is designed to predict the physiological requirements needed to maintain thermal balance under specified environmental conditions.

Together, these components provide a flexible framework for linking climate to physiological performance and species distributions. However, as a point-based modelling system, NicheMapR is typically applied at individual locations rather than across spatial grids.

The package is extensively tested and documented and instructions detailed instructions for downloading, installing and using it are provided [here](https://mrke.github.io/).

### TrenchR

The TrenchR package (Buckley *et al.* 2023) provides a set of functions for modelling thermal environments and organismal heat exchange, primarily aimed at teaching and exploratory analyses. It implements relatively simple and modular microclimate and biophysical calculations, allowing users to examine how environmental conditions influence body temperature and heat fluxes under different scenarios.

Unlike NicheMapR and the workflow described in this vignette, TrenchR does not provide a fully integrated microclimate modelling framework. Instead, it offers modular functions for calculating individual processes (e.g. radiative and convective heat exchange), typically using simplified formulations. This makes it a useful educational resource, as assumptions and parameter dependencies are transparent and easy to explore.

A major strength of the package is its close integration with the open online textbook *Physical Processes in Ecosystems* by Buckley and colleagues. The book provides an accessible introduction to the physical principles underpinning ecological and microclimate processes, including radiation balance, heat transfer, mass transfer, fluid dynamics and organismal energy balance. TrenchR functions are used extensively throughout the text to demonstrate and explore these concepts interactively in R, making the package especially valuable for teaching and for developing intuition about how environmental and physiological processes interact.

The book is available here: <https://bookdown.org/huckley/Physical_Processes_In_Ecosystems/>

However, the representation of environmental conditions is relatively crude. In particular, TrenchR does not explicitly resolve below-canopy microclimate or coupled soil–vegetation–atmosphere processes, and is therefore less suited to spatially explicit or process-rich applications across heterogeneous landscapes.

Further details can be found here: <https://trenchproject.github.io/TrenchR/>

The package can also be installed from CRAN:

```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages("TrenchR")
library(TrenchR)
```
